children: At least two foreign manufacturers of polymer currency and an Indian substrate maker in partnership with UK-based banknote manufacturer De La Rue have submitted bids in response to a global Expression of Interest (EOI) floated by Reserve Bank of India subsidiary Bharatiya Reserve Bank Note Mudran (P) Ltd (BRBNMPL), an Indian Express report said on Monday.
The EOI had set August 18 as the deadline for submissions.

The companies bidding for the EOI have been required to sign an integrity pact, confidentiality agreement, no-agent pact and an undertaking to firewall their Indian operations from any operations they may have in China and Pakistan, given the sensitivity around future supplies of polymer banknotes, The Indian Express said.

Bidders have also had to certify that the polymer substrate they supply to BRBNMPL will not contain animal tallow or its DNA. The Indian Express reported that concerns over animal tallow in banknotes in countries such as the UK are believed to be among the reasons for the RBI's reluctance to introduce polymer currency in India.

The BRBNMPL EOI documents flagged an "immediate" requirement for around 68,000 reams of polymer substrate for printing Indian banknotes, The Indian Express reported. Each ream is required to contain 500 sheets of polymer film, with bidders also required to submit samples.

The samples will be tested across different climatic zones, following which eligible bidders will be allowed to participate in the final BRBNMPL tender. A corrigendum issued before the August 18 deadline clarified that bidders did not need to submit proof of their financial standing at this "qualifying" stage, The Indian Express said.

Cosmo First, described by The Indian Express as the largest Indian exporter of BOPP (biaxially oriented polypropylene) and a major supplier to De La Rue, is among the companies in the running. De La Rue, which describes itself as the world's largest banknote supplier, has said it has helped several countries transition to polymer banknotes, which it describes as cleaner, greener, more secure and durable.

According to industry sources cited by The Indian Express, Cosmo First has named De La Rue as its "technical partner", with the UK company set to provide security features for its polymer substrate as required by BRBNMPL.

Australia-based CCL Secure is another foreign company that has submitted a bid, The Indian Express reported. The company is a major polymer banknote supplier and currently provides polymer solutions to 40 central banks. It highlights anti-counterfeiting features and claims polymer banknotes can last six times longer than cotton-based currency paper.

CCL Secure's website says it provides countries with solutions combining polymer-based banknotes with conventional currency paper made from cotton pulp. The Indian Express reported that this is the model the RBI is currently considering for India, with polymer banknotes initially proposed for Rs 10 and Rs 20 denominations.

Vietnam was among the countries that imported polymer substrate from CCL Secure. However, three years ago, Hanoi-based Q&T Hi-tech Polymer Company Limited began domestic banknote supplies and claimed a 78% lifecycle saving over cotton paper currency. The company is now expanding beyond Vietnam and, according to industry sources cited by The Indian Express, has also bid for the BRBNMPL EOI.

title: RBI's plastic note plan draws Cosmo First, CCL Secure; no animal tallow, China-Pakistan firewall mandatory: Report
